scope: Curated educational guides and selected references; not a systematic or exhaustive review. Biological mechanisms do not by themselves prove clinical benefit. Nutrient requirements, deficiency treatment and routine supplement use are different questions. Research does not endorse catalog brands. Individual and pediatric care require appropriate professional guidance; international findings may not generalize to every Indian product or population.

articles.title: Protein supplements: total intake, training and label quality
articles.summary: A powder is one way to supply dietary protein. The useful comparison starts with actual protein content and the training context.
articles.evidence: Trial syntheses support modest additional gains when protein supplementation accompanies resistance training. The benefit depends on the wider diet and training programme.
articles.limitations: Trials do not establish that every whey, plant or fermented product has the same effect. A price ranking is not a ranking of digestibility, amino-acid quality or clinical benefit.
articles.catalogReading: Use cost per gram of labelled protein rather than cost per gram of powder. Check serving size, concentration, ingredient source and label evidence separately.
articles.safety: Check food allergens and individual dietary restrictions. People with medically restricted protein intake need individual advice.
articles.author: Supplement Research editorial synthesis
bodySteps: Stomach and intestinal enzymes break dietary protein into smaller peptides and amino acids.
The small intestine absorbs these building blocks into circulation.
Tissues use amino acids to make proteins; resistance training provides a stimulus for muscle adaptation.
articles.treatment: Protein supplementation can help address inadequate intake within a nutrition plan. Powder alone does not cure muscle wasting or an illness causing poor nutrition.
articles.whoMayBenefit: People unable to meet assessed protein needs through food, including some athletes or people receiving supervised nutritional care.
articles.routineUse: Everyone needs dietary protein; everyone does not need protein powder. Reassess the food gap rather than assuming lifelong use.

articles.title: Creatine: why the studied form matters
articles.summary: Monohydrate has an extensive exercise-research base; premium names and smaller portions do not establish superiority.
articles.evidence: Research supports creatine monohydrate for repeated high-intensity work and some resistance-training adaptations.
articles.limitations: Evidence is strongest for particular outcomes and studied protocols. It cannot automatically be transferred to HCl, nitrate or a proprietary blend.
articles.catalogReading: The catalog compares labelled compound mass. Equal grams of different creatine salts are not assumed chemically equivalent; micronization describes processing rather than proven greater efficacy.
articles.safety: Discuss use with a clinician if you have kidney disease or another relevant medical condition. Research protocols are not personalized instructions.
articles.author: Supplement Research editorial synthesis
bodySteps: Absorbed creatine enters circulation and is taken up by tissues, predominantly muscle.
Some is stored as phosphocreatine, which helps rapidly regenerate ATP during intense effort.
Creatine and phosphocreatine gradually form creatinine, which the kidneys excrete.
articles.treatment: A performance aid is not a cure for weakness, fatigue or a neurological disease. Specialist uses require condition-specific evidence and care.
articles.whoMayBenefit: Adults doing repeated high-intensity efforts or resistance training who want an optional performance aid.
articles.routineUse: No universal requirement for a creatine supplement. Healthy bodies make creatine, and it is also obtained from some foods.

articles.title: Ashwagandha: promising short trials, uncertain equivalence
articles.summary: Stress and sleep findings need to be read alongside extract identity, standardization and trial duration.
articles.evidence: Some small randomized trials report improvements in stress measures and sleep with specific preparations.
articles.limitations: Short follow-up, small samples and heterogeneous extracts limit certainty. Results for a standardized root extract do not establish the same benefit for whole root powder or a blend.
articles.catalogReading: Compare the same material class. Withanolide mass can be calculated only when both the standardized extract mass and percentage are verified. A headline milligram figure may represent a different basis.
articles.safety: Liver injury has been reported, and thyroid effects and drug interactions are concerns. Avoid use in pregnancy; seek professional advice for relevant conditions or medicines.
articles.author: Supplement Research editorial synthesis
bodySteps: A swallowed product supplies a mixture of plant constituents; powders and extracts can have different compositions.
Absorption and metabolism depend on the preparation. Human studies do not establish one uniform pathway for all products.
Proposed stress-response mechanisms do not prove a clinical benefit; withanolide percentage is not a measure of cure.
articles.treatment: No established cure for anxiety disorders, insomnia or thyroid disease. Persistent symptoms need assessment rather than self-treatment with an extract.
articles.whoMayBenefit: Some adults seeking short-term stress or sleep support may consider a specific studied preparation after reviewing risks and alternatives.
articles.routineUse: No group should assume it is essential or a lifelong supplement. Long-term safety is uncertain.

articles.title: Fish oil: EPA+DHA, outcomes and the prescription distinction
articles.summary: Total fish-oil mass is not the same as the amount of EPA and DHA. More oil does not by itself establish greater benefit.
articles.evidence: Omega-3 research differs by population and preparation. VITAL did not show a significant reduction in its primary cardiovascular or cancer outcomes with the tested marine omega-3 supplement.
articles.limitations: Specific prescription formulations, high-risk patients and treatment of high triglycerides address different questions from routine retail supplementation.
articles.catalogReading: Use verified EPA+DHA per label serving and cost per common active amount. Keep total oil, chemical form, serving count and stock status visible.
articles.safety: Discuss use with a clinician when taking anticoagulants or considering high doses. High-dose trials have raised atrial-fibrillation concerns in some settings.
articles.author: Supplement Research editorial synthesis
bodySteps: Digestion releases fatty acids from dietary oils.
Intestinal cells package absorbed fats into transport particles that reach the circulation through lymph.
EPA and DHA enter tissue lipids and cell membranes and contribute to signalling pathways.
articles.treatment: Prescription omega-3 medicines can treat high triglycerides under medical care. Retail fish oil is not an interchangeable prescription or a cure for heart disease.
articles.whoMayBenefit: People with a clinician-established indication; those with low fish intake can first review food and suitable alternative omega-3 sources.
articles.routineUse: No blanket recommendation that every healthy adult needs fish-oil capsules. Dietary context and the clinical goal matter.

articles.title: Vitamin D: deficiency treatment versus routine supplementation
articles.summary: Strength is a unit of amount, not a promise of improved health. The reason for taking vitamin D matters.
articles.evidence: Vitamin D supports calcium regulation and bone health. In generally healthy adults not selected for deficiency, the VITAL fracture study did not demonstrate fewer fractures from supplementation.
articles.limitations: This finding should not be generalized to treatment of diagnosed deficiency or specific bone disorders. A high-strength product is not automatically a better choice.
articles.catalogReading: The catalog shows IU and micrograms together: 1 microgram equals 40 IU. Read the serving size and intended product directions; the comparison unit is not a recommended daily amount.
articles.safety: Excess vitamin D can cause harm, including high blood calcium. Consider existing prescriptions and other supplements before combining products.
articles.author: Supplement Research editorial synthesis
bodySteps: The intestine absorbs vitamin D from food or supplements; skin can also produce it after UVB exposure.
The liver converts it to 25-hydroxyvitamin D, the main blood marker of status.
The kidneys produce its active hormone form, which helps regulate calcium absorption and bone mineral balance.
articles.treatment: Correcting vitamin D deficiency can treat deficiency-related rickets or osteomalacia. It is not a general cure for fatigue, cancer or infections.
articles.whoMayBenefit: People with established deficiency or malabsorption may need treatment. Some groups have routine preventive guidance, including breastfed infants; a pediatric clinician should guide this, not adult catalog strengths.
articles.routineUse: Some people need ongoing supplementation, but the indication and plan differ. A higher-risk group is not proof of an individual deficiency.

articles.title: Magnesium: elemental amounts before salt names
articles.summary: Glycinate, citrate and oxide describe compounds. Their full mass must not be mistaken for elemental magnesium.
articles.evidence: Magnesium is an essential nutrient; the evidence and relevance of supplementation depend on the indication and baseline nutritional status.
articles.limitations: Absorption differences between forms do not, by themselves, establish superiority for sleep or athletic recovery. Broad wellness claims need outcome-specific trials.
articles.catalogReading: Compare explicitly labelled elemental magnesium per serving. The site keeps compound mass separate and withholds active-content cost when elemental amounts or serving size are unclear.
articles.safety: Supplemental magnesium can cause diarrhoea and interact with some medicines. Kidney impairment changes safety considerations; seek individual advice.
articles.author: Supplement Research editorial synthesis
bodySteps: A magnesium compound must release magnesium that can be absorbed from the intestine.
Absorbed magnesium supports enzyme activity, energy metabolism, and normal nerve and muscle function.
The kidneys help regulate magnesium balance by adjusting excretion.
articles.treatment: Replacement treats magnesium deficiency when indicated. Some magnesium medicines act as laxatives or antacids; this does not make every supplement a treatment for constipation, insomnia or cramps.
articles.whoMayBenefit: People with a diagnosed deficiency or an assessed intake or absorption problem, with attention to kidney function and medicines.
articles.routineUse: No universal need for magnesium tablets if intake is adequate. Symptoms such as cramps alone do not establish deficiency.

articles.title: ZMC: assess zinc, magnesium and calcium separately
articles.summary: A three-mineral tablet is a formulation choice, not a single active ingredient with one meaningful strength score.
articles.evidence: Each mineral has established nutritional roles. Evidence about individual nutrients does not demonstrate that every ZMC combination improves outcomes.
articles.limitations: This guide makes no combination-specific efficacy claim. Product ratios, baseline diet, clinical need and co-ingredients differ; ZMA studies are not evidence for calcium-containing ZMC products.
articles.catalogReading: Review the elemental amount of each mineral, the label serving and its cost. Do not add their masses into a combined value score or treat calcium-salt weight as elemental calcium.
articles.safety: Check overlapping supplements and medicines. Excess zinc can affect copper status; calcium and magnesium can interfere with absorption of some medicines.
articles.author: Supplement Research editorial synthesis
bodySteps: The tablet releases separate calcium, magnesium and zinc compounds in the digestive tract.
Intestinal absorption and regulation differ for each mineral; vitamin D supports active calcium absorption.
Calcium supports bone and signalling functions, magnesium supports enzyme activity, and zinc supports many cellular processes.
articles.treatment: An appropriate individual mineral can correct its deficiency. This is not evidence that a ZMC combination cures osteoporosis, low testosterone or a general immunity problem.
articles.whoMayBenefit: Someone with assessed needs for the included minerals may consider a combination if its amounts fit the plan; a single deficient nutrient may need a different product.
articles.routineUse: No universal requirement for a three-mineral stack. Review each mineral separately and check overlap with other supplements.

articles.title: Glutathione: antioxidant biology versus supplement promises
articles.summary: Your cells make glutathione. An important biological role does not prove that buying an oral supplement prevents disease or changes skin tone.
articles.evidence: Oral trials show mixed biomarker results: a six-month study reported higher body stores, while a four-week study found no improvement in measured oxidative-stress markers. Small skin studies report some changes in melanin indices; a 2026 trial also had mixed outcomes. These results do not establish broad health benefits.
articles.limitations: Studies differ in formulation, duration and outcome. A biomarker or cosmetic measurement is not a demonstrated reduction in illness. Lasting benefits and long-term safety remain uncertain; reduced, S-acetyl, liposomal and blended products should not be assumed equivalent.
articles.catalogReading: Compare the declared glutathione amount per verified label serving, ingredient form, pack servings and cost within the same formulation. Total blend weight, vitamin C, NAC and cysteine are not glutathione mass. A liposomal or reduced claim alone does not prove better clinical results.
articles.safety: The cited small adult trials cannot establish safety for indefinite use, pregnancy, breastfeeding or children. Review medicines, medical conditions and co-ingredients with a qualified clinician. Oral findings cannot be transferred to injections; this catalog covers oral products and does not recommend intravenous use.
articles.author: Supplement Research editorial synthesis
bodySteps: Glutathione is a small peptide made from glutamate, cysteine and glycine. Digestion, uptake and processing influence what an oral formulation delivers; the label amount is not a measured amount reaching a tissue.
Cells synthesize and recycle their own glutathione. Together with enzymes, it participates in antioxidant reactions and redox regulation.
Supplement studies measure changes in blood or other samples, but greater measured glutathione does not automatically mean better health, less ageing or lighter skin.
articles.treatment: The selected oral trials do not establish a cure for liver disease, cancer or a pigmentation disorder, or a general detox treatment. A new or changing skin patch needs assessment rather than assuming a supplement will correct it.
articles.whoMayBenefit: Adults considering a specific cosmetic goal can discuss the limited findings and alternatives with a dermatologist. These sources do not identify a healthy group that should routinely take glutathione; disease-specific use requires separate clinical evidence.
articles.routineUse: There is no established universal need for an oral glutathione supplement. The body makes it, and adequate nutrition supports its metabolism. Changing a laboratory marker is not a reason by itself to continue indefinitely.

articles.title: Melatonin: body-clock timing before stronger sleep products
articles.summary: Melatonin is a hormone involved in the sleep-wake cycle. The reason, timing and release profile matter more than choosing the largest milligram number.
articles.evidence: Evidence is more relevant to circadian problems such as jet lag and some delayed sleep-wake phase cases than to all poor sleep. In a four-week trial, clinically assessed delayed-phase patients improved with melatonin plus behavioural scheduling. AASM suggests against using melatonin for chronic adult insomnia; CBT-I is an initial treatment to discuss.
articles.limitations: Short trials and specific sleep disorders do not establish benefit for every sleep complaint. Long-term safety remains uncertain. A gummy, strip, immediate-release tablet and prolonged-release product cannot be assumed to give the same exposure or outcome.
articles.catalogReading: Read melatonin milligrams per verified label serving, units per serving and release description. Keep other sedating ingredients separate. Cost per common milligram amount is a price calculation, not an intake recommendation, and more melatonin is not automatically better.
articles.safety: Possible effects include daytime drowsiness, headache and dizziness. Do not drive or use machinery when drowsy. Review medicines, especially blood thinners, and epilepsy with a clinician. Pregnancy and breastfeeding safety data are limited. Children need pediatric guidance; keep every form, including gummies, out of reach.
articles.author: Supplement Research editorial synthesis
bodySteps: Darkness normally promotes melatonin release from the brain's pineal gland, providing a biological night-time signal; evening light can suppress this signal.

Swallowed melatonin is absorbed and undergoes substantial first-pass processing in the liver. Different release systems can change its exposure pattern; milligram content alone does not describe that pattern.
Melatonin acts at receptors involved in sleep and circadian regulation. The effect depends on the sleep problem and timing; taking a product does not diagnose a low melatonin level.
articles.treatment: Melatonin can form part of professionally planned care for selected circadian disorders. It is not a cure for chronic insomnia, stress or sleep apnoea. Persistent poor sleep or excessive daytime sleepiness warrants assessment of its cause.
articles.whoMayBenefit: Some people with jet lag or a clinically assessed circadian delay may benefit from an appropriate plan. Children with sleep disorders require pediatric assessment, not selection from adult retail strengths. A short night of sleep alone does not establish a need.
articles.routineUse: No one should assume they need nightly melatonin indefinitely. Review the indication, sleep schedule and continuing benefit with a clinician. Behavioural treatment and light/sleep timing can be central, and melatonin is not an automatic addition to a sleep stack.

articles.title: Biotin: hair claims, dietary needs and laboratory tests
articles.summary: Biotin is vitamin B7. Correcting a deficiency is different from assuming that more biotin will improve healthy hair or nails.
articles.evidence: Established biotin deficiency can respond to appropriate treatment. Evidence for routine hair, skin and nail benefits in people without deficiency is limited, relying largely on small studies and case reports.
articles.limitations: Hair or nail symptoms alone do not establish biotin deficiency. A larger labelled amount does not demonstrate better cosmetic results in an adequately nourished person.
articles.catalogReading: Check biotin micrograms per verified label serving, units per serving and other ingredients. Milligrams and micrograms are different units: 1 mg equals 1,000 micrograms. Compare equal labelled amounts without turning strength into a hair-growth score.
articles.safety: Tell the clinician and laboratory about every biotin-containing product before blood testing, including hair gummies and multivitamins. Some assays can give misleading thyroid results or falsely low troponin results. Ask the testing team for assay-specific instructions; there is no universal stopping interval for every test.
articles.author: Supplement Research editorial synthesis
bodySteps: Digestion releases food-bound biotin; the enzyme biotinidase helps make free biotin available for intestinal absorption.
Cells use biotin with enzymes involved in processing fats, carbohydrates and amino acids.
Supporting normal metabolism does not mean that an additional high-strength supplement improves hair when biotin supply is already adequate.
articles.treatment: Confirmed deficiency and rare inherited biotinidase disorders require an appropriate clinical plan. A retail hair product is not a diagnosis or a general treatment for hair loss.
articles.whoMayBenefit: People with an established deficiency or a specific metabolic disorder may need supervised supplementation. A risk factor or cosmetic concern should prompt assessment rather than automatically selecting the strongest pack.
articles.routineUse: Many foods supply biotin. A high-strength beauty supplement is not a universal requirement. Reassess the reason for taking it and include biotin from combination products when discussing laboratory tests.

articles.title: Vitamin C: deficiency, absorption and everyday claims
articles.summary: Vitamin C supports normal body functions, but the largest tablet or an immunity claim does not establish the greatest benefit.
articles.evidence: Vitamin C is needed for collagen formation and helps absorb non-heme iron. Routine supplementation generally does not prevent common colds in the wider population; regular use may modestly shorten their duration.
articles.limitations: Absorption becomes less efficient at larger oral intakes. Biological antioxidant or immune roles do not establish that every supplement prevents illness. Price and labelled milligrams do not measure clinical benefit.
articles.catalogReading: Use the declared vitamin C amount per verified serving, not the whole weight of an ascorbate salt, fruit extract or blend. Read added zinc, sweeteners and other ingredients separately. An effervescent or liposomal label alone does not establish superiority.
articles.safety: Large supplemental amounts can cause diarrhoea, nausea and abdominal discomfort. People with kidney disease, hyperoxaluria or iron-overload conditions should discuss use with a clinician. Review medicines and overlapping products; population upper limits are safety boundaries rather than intake goals.
articles.author: Supplement Research editorial synthesis
bodySteps: Vitamin C is absorbed through the intestine; the fraction absorbed falls as oral intake becomes larger.
Tissues use it in enzyme reactions, including collagen formation, and antioxidant functions.
Kidneys excrete absorbed vitamin C that is not retained, so a higher label amount is not the amount delivered to a target tissue.
articles.treatment: Scurvy is severe vitamin C deficiency and needs treatment and attention to its dietary cause. Correcting deficiency does not make vitamin C a cure for every infection or a replacement for assessment of persistent symptoms.
articles.whoMayBenefit: People whose diets cannot supply adequate vitamin C, including those with markedly restricted food intake, may need nutrition support. A clinician can assess suspected deficiency and a suitable approach.
articles.routineUse: Everyone needs dietary vitamin C; everyone does not need a daily supplement. Fruit and vegetables can supply it. If a supplement addresses a dietary gap, review the gap rather than escalating strength indefinitely.

articles.title: B vitamins: individual nutrients, individual requirements
articles.summary: Vitamin B is a family of eight nutrients. A B-complex product is a formulation, not one active ingredient with a meaningful combined strength.
articles.evidence: B vitamins have distinct roles in metabolism, blood-cell production and nervous-system function. Replacing a deficient vitamin can be useful; vague tiredness alone does not identify which nutrient, if any, is lacking.
articles.limitations: B1, B2, B3, B5, B6, B7, B9 and B12 are not interchangeable. Benefits from treating one deficiency cannot be transferred to every B-complex formulation, energy claim or premium chemical form.
articles.catalogReading: Compare each vitamin amount and chemical form on the same label-serving basis. B7 is biotin and B9 is folate; their dedicated guides add context. Keep milligrams, micrograms and folate DFE distinct. The catalog uses serving cost rather than adding B-vitamin masses into a potency score.
articles.safety: Excess supplemental B6 can damage sensory nerves. Nicotinic acid can cause flushing and, at high exposure, other serious effects; nicotinamide has a different risk profile. Check all overlapping products and medicines. Water-soluble does not mean unlimited amounts are harmless.
articles.author: Supplement Research editorial synthesis
bodySteps: Different B vitamins enter distinct metabolic pathways; there is no single absorption or processing route for a B-complex blend.

For food-bound B12, digestive processing releases the vitamin before it binds intrinsic factor for absorption in the small intestine. Absorption problems can therefore matter even when intake appears adequate.
Cells use different B-derived coenzymes in energy metabolism and other functions. A physiological role does not establish that extra vitamins improve performance in someone with adequate status.
articles.treatment: B12 deficiency, other B-vitamin deficiencies and anaemia need cause-specific care. Numbness, persistent fatigue or suspected malabsorption should not be managed solely by choosing an energy supplement.
articles.whoMayBenefit: People eating little or no animal food need a reliable B12 source, such as appropriately fortified foods or supplementation. Older adults and people with certain gastrointestinal conditions or medicines may also need assessment. These are reasons to review needs, not automatic diagnoses.
articles.routineUse: Choose a plan around the specific dietary or clinical need. A B-complex is not automatically better than a targeted nutrient. Review continuing use, overlapping B6 or niacin, and any other products containing biotin or folate.

articles.title: Folic acid and folate: forms, labels and pregnancy planning
articles.summary: Folate is vitamin B9. Folic acid, methylfolate and dietary folate equivalents describe different forms or measurement bases.
articles.evidence: Folate supports DNA synthesis and cell division. Folic acid before and during early pregnancy helps prevent neural tube defects; CDC identifies folic acid as the form demonstrated to provide this protection.
articles.limitations: A methylfolate or active-form claim does not establish the same birth-defect-prevention evidence. A label in micrograms DFE is not the same as micrograms of folic acid. The catalog does not infer a universal conversion across forms.
articles.catalogReading: Record folic acid, methylfolate and declared folate DFE separately on the verified label-serving basis. Primary folic-acid costs require an explicit folic acid quantity; methylfolate mass is not relabelled as folic acid. Check prenatal, B-complex and standalone products for overlap.
articles.safety: Large amounts of folic acid can correct the anaemia of B12 deficiency while its neurological injury remains unaddressed. Review B12 status when clinically appropriate and discuss medicines, including antifolate or antiseizure treatment, with a clinician. Do not alter prescribed treatment from a catalog comparison.
articles.author: Supplement Research editorial synthesis
bodySteps: Food folates, folic acid and supplemental 5-MTHF enter the diet in different chemical forms; their label masses do not directly describe identical availability.
The body uses folate coenzymes to transfer one-carbon groups needed for DNA synthesis and amino-acid metabolism.
Adequate folate is especially important during rapid cell division. Folic acid prevention before and in early pregnancy addresses a specific developmental risk, not every possible birth defect.
articles.treatment: Folate-deficiency anaemia needs an assessment of its cause and of possible B12 deficiency. Preventing neural tube defects is different from treating an established defect or curing infertility.
articles.whoMayBenefit: Women who could become pregnant should follow a folic-acid prevention plan; waiting until pregnancy is recognised can miss part of the relevant period. Confirm the plan with an appropriate clinician, particularly after a previous affected pregnancy or when medicines alter folate requirements.
articles.routineUse: This is an important population-specific prevention recommendation, not a universal reason for everyone to buy a folate product. Pregnancy care may require a broader plan. The stack builder provides education and does not select an adult retail strength as a pregnancy prescription.

sources.title: NIH ODS: Exercise and athletic performance
sources.summary: Reviews protein and creatine in exercise, including differences between studied ingredients and marketing claims.
sources.limitations: A broad reference, not an independent test of products in this catalog.

sources.title: Morton et al.: Protein supplementation and resistance training
sources.summary: Across 49 trials involving 1,863 participants, protein supplements modestly improved training-related gains in strength and fat-free mass.
sources.limitations: Healthy adults undertaking resistance training; results do not establish that one commercial brand is superior.

sources.title: Kreider et al.: ISSN creatine position stand
sources.summary: Reviews evidence supporting creatine monohydrate for repeated high-intensity exercise and training adaptations.
sources.limitations: A narrative position statement, not a head-to-head trial of every form. Read the authors’ disclosed commercial relationships.

sources.title: NIH ODS: Ashwagandha for stress, anxiety and sleep
sources.summary: Small, short trials suggest possible improvements in stress and sleep, with substantial variation in extracts and study methods.
sources.limitations: Long-term safety and the best preparation remain uncertain. Liver, thyroid and medication concerns require attention.

sources.title: Chandrasekhar et al.: Ashwagandha root extract and stress
sources.summary: A 60-day placebo-controlled study enrolled 64 adults with chronic stress and reported improved stress measures with a specific root extract.
sources.limitations: Small and short; findings do not establish equivalence for root powders, other extracts, or blends.

sources.title: NIH ODS: Omega-3 fatty acids
sources.summary: Reviews EPA and DHA, dietary sources, cardiovascular research and safety. Outcomes depend on the preparation and clinical context.
sources.limitations: Prescription omega-3 treatments and ordinary retail fish oil are not interchangeable evidence.

sources.title: Manson et al.: Marine omega-3s in the VITAL trial
sources.summary: In 25,871 US adults, marine omega-3 supplementation did not significantly lower the primary major cardiovascular-event or invasive-cancer outcomes.
sources.limitations: Primary prevention in older adults; secondary outcomes and other populations require separate interpretation.

sources.title: NIH ODS: Vitamin D
sources.summary: Explains vitamin D status, bone health, deficiency, units and evidence on supplementation.
sources.limitations: Correcting deficiency and routinely supplementing generally healthy adults are different questions.

sources.title: LeBoff et al.: Vitamin D and incident fractures
sources.summary: In the VITAL ancillary fracture trial, vitamin D did not significantly reduce fractures in generally healthy midlife and older adults.
sources.limitations: Participants were not selected for deficiency, low bone mass or osteoporosis; this does not negate treatment for a diagnosed need.

sources.title: NIH ODS: Magnesium
sources.summary: Explains elemental magnesium, differences in salt forms, absorption, deficiency and safety.
sources.limitations: A chemical form or absorption claim alone does not prove better sleep, recovery or other clinical outcomes.

sources.title: NIH ODS: Calcium
sources.summary: Covers calcium requirements, elemental content, bone-health research and supplement considerations.
sources.limitations: Benefits depend on dietary intake and population; a larger compound mass is not necessarily more elemental calcium.

sources.title: NIH ODS: Zinc
sources.summary: Explains zinc functions, deficiency, excess intake and interactions.
sources.limitations: Evidence for one nutrient or indication does not validate a combined ZMC product.

sources.title: NIDDK: Your digestive system and how it works
sources.summary: Explains how digestion breaks proteins into amino acids and how the small intestine absorbs nutrients.
sources.limitations: Basic physiology does not establish the effectiveness of a supplement or commercial product.

sources.title: Wu et al.: Glutathione metabolism and nutritional context
sources.summary: Explains cellular synthesis from glutamate, cysteine and glycine, redox functions and the importance of adequate protein nutrition.
sources.limitations: Biological roles and disease associations do not establish that oral supplementation improves clinical outcomes.

sources.title: Richie et al.: Oral glutathione and body stores
sources.summary: A six-month placebo-controlled study in 54 healthy nonsmokers reported higher glutathione concentrations in several sampled body compartments.
sources.limitations: Biomarker changes do not establish disease prevention, a detox treatment or benefit for every formulation.

sources.title: Allen and Bradley: Oral glutathione and oxidative-stress markers
sources.summary: Forty healthy adults entered a four-week placebo-controlled study; glutathione status and measured oxidative-stress markers did not significantly improve.
sources.limitations: Short follow-up and healthy volunteers limit generalization; this trial and longer studies address different exposure periods.

sources.title: Arjinpathana and Asawanonda: Oral glutathione and skin melanin indices
sources.summary: A four-week trial in 60 healthy medical students found statistically greater melanin-index reductions than placebo at two of six measured sites.
sources.limitations: A small cosmetic study does not establish lasting skin-lightening, treatment of a pigmentation disorder or long-term safety. Published in 2012; online in 2010.

sources.title: Kusumawardani et al.: S-acetyl versus reduced glutathione for skin measures
sources.summary: A 12-week study randomized 90 women to S-acetyl glutathione, reduced glutathione or placebo. Some melanin-index analyses favored treatment, while measured pigmentation scores and blood glutathione did not differ significantly between groups.
sources.limitations: Baseline melanin indices differed; the small, selected population, short follow-up and mixed outcomes limit claims of general or lasting superiority.

sources.title: NCCIH: Melatonin, usefulness and safety
sources.summary: Distinguishes circadian uses such as jet lag from chronic insomnia, and reviews adverse effects, medicine interactions and limited long-term safety data.
sources.limitations: This US reference does not establish Indian regulatory status, prove a catalog product matches its label or support unsupervised pediatric use.

sources.title: Sletten et al.: Melatonin with behavioural scheduling for delayed sleep phase
sources.summary: A four-week trial randomized 116 clinically assessed delayed-sleep-phase patients. Melatonin combined with behavioural sleep scheduling improved sleep initiation compared with placebo and scheduling.
sources.limitations: Selected circadian-delay patients and a combined intervention; no evidence here for every sleep complaint, catalog strength or long-term treatment.

sources.title: AASM: Pharmacologic treatment guideline for chronic insomnia in adults
sources.summary: The guideline suggests against melatonin for adult sleep-onset or sleep-maintenance insomnia, reflecting weak and limited evidence for that indication.
sources.limitations: A weak recommendation addressing chronic insomnia; it is not a recommendation against all circadian-disorder uses.

sources.title: AASM: Melatonin use in children and adolescents
sources.summary: Recommends pediatric professional advice, attention to sleep habits, and keeping melatonin out of children's reach. Notes that supplement content can differ from labels.
sources.limitations: Label-variation evidence cited in the advisory is not independent testing of Indian catalog products.

sources.title: Lane and Moss: First-pass hepatic metabolism of melatonin
sources.summary: Analysis of human oral and intravenous data identified substantial liver extraction and reduced systemic availability after swallowing melatonin.
sources.limitations: An older pharmacokinetic analysis explains exposure; it does not compare modern release systems or prove clinical superiority.

sources.title: NIDDK LiverTox: Melatonin physiology
sources.summary: Describes pineal production, night-time secretion and action at melatonin receptors involved in sleep-wake regulation.
sources.limitations: Physiological signalling does not by itself establish that a supplement is necessary or effective for an individual.

sources.title: NIH ODS: Biotin, nutrition and evidence for hair claims
sources.summary: Explains biotin metabolism, rare deficiency and the limited evidence behind hair, skin and nail supplement claims.
sources.limitations: Deficiency treatment and case reports do not establish cosmetic benefits for adequately nourished consumers.

sources.title: FDA: Biotin interference with troponin laboratory tests
sources.summary: Warns that biotin can distort susceptible laboratory assays, including falsely low troponin results used in heart-attack assessment.
sources.limitations: Interference depends on the assay and exposure; the page does not provide a universal safe interval before every blood test.

sources.title: NIH ODS: Vitamin C, absorption and clinical evidence
sources.summary: Reviews dose-dependent absorption, physiological roles, cold research, adverse effects and medicine interactions.
sources.limitations: A nutrient role is not proof that a particular retail formulation prevents disease or outperforms dietary sources.

sources.title: NHS: Vitamin C, food sources and supplement cautions
sources.summary: Describes food sources, deficiency and gastrointestinal effects of excessive supplemental vitamin C.
sources.limitations: UK population guidance is not an individual prescription or evidence that Indian catalog products match their labels.

sources.title: NHS: The B-vitamin family and folic acid
sources.summary: Distinguishes individual B vitamins, their dietary roles and the risks of treating the family as one interchangeable nutrient.
sources.limitations: General dietary guidance does not diagnose the cause of fatigue or establish a need for a B-complex product.

sources.title: NIH ODS: Vitamin B12 absorption and deficiency risk
sources.summary: Explains intrinsic-factor-dependent absorption, deficiency, plant-based dietary risk, gastrointestinal causes and medicine effects.
sources.limitations: Risk factors do not diagnose deficiency; oral retail products are not a substitute for assessing absorption disorders or neurological symptoms.

sources.title: NIH ODS: Vitamin B6 and excessive-intake neuropathy
sources.summary: Reviews vitamin B6 functions, medicines and sensory-nerve injury associated with excessive supplemental exposure.
sources.limitations: Upper limits differ between authorities and are not treatment targets. Total intake from overlapping products matters.

sources.title: NIH ODS: Niacin forms and high-intake safety
sources.summary: Distinguishes nicotinic acid from nicotinamide and explains flushing, other adverse effects and medically supervised uses.
sources.limitations: Different niacin forms have different effects. Supplement pricing does not establish treatment equivalence or justify high-dose use.

sources.title: NIH ODS: Folate forms, dietary folate equivalents and safety
sources.summary: Explains food folate, folic acid and 5-MTHF; dietary folate equivalents reflect a different basis from ingredient mass.
sources.limitations: DFE conversion depends on context, and established conversion factors for supplemental 5-MTHF are lacking. Forms are not treated as identical in the catalog.

sources.title: CDC: Folic acid and prevention of neural tube defects
sources.summary: Recommends folic acid for women who could become pregnant and identifies it as the folate form shown to prevent neural tube defects.
sources.limitations: This general public-health recommendation is not an individual pregnancy plan or proof that every folate form has the same prevention evidence.

sources.title: GeneReviews: Biotinidase deficiency and targeted care
sources.summary: Describes diagnosis and specialist treatment of an inherited biotin-recycling disorder.
sources.limitations: Lifelong therapy for a diagnosed genetic disorder does not support routine high-strength biotin for cosmetic concerns.

sources.title: Hemila and Chalker: Vitamin C for preventing and treating the common cold
sources.summary: Placebo-controlled trial synthesis found no general-population reduction in cold incidence, with modestly shorter colds during regular supplementation.
sources.limitations: Trials differ in population and protocol; these findings do not establish prevention by every formulation or benefit from starting after symptoms begin.
